title: The blessing
hookLine: the service ends in a blessing, often Numbers 6:24–26

lines: A HAND RAISED OVER THE ROOM.
cards: Coats are half on. The last hymn is over. A toddler is making a break for the door, and someone is checking a phone.
Then the minister raises a hand over the room, or both hands, palms out, and the shuffling stops. Heads bow. Into the quiet come words from the book of Numbers: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee."
A few more lines, an amen, and the doors open onto the parking lot and the rest of the week. Before anyone reaches the car, something has been spoken over them. Today's word is benediction.

teach.b: You met these lines on day four hundred three. Today, where they land: at the door. A benediction is a blessing spoken over people, and a service often closes with one.
One often used comes from Numbers. God tells Moses to speak to Aaron and his sons: "On this wise ye shall bless the children of Israel."

Then: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Kept, shone upon, given peace.
These were Israel's words first, and Jews pray them still. Notice who is blessing.
The next verse says the priests "shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them." The raised hands pass the blessing on; in the text, God is the one who blesses.
In Leviticus, after the offerings, "Aaron lifted up his hand toward the people, and blessed them."

Near the end of Luke, out near Bethany, Jesus "lifted up his hands, and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them." Their last sight of him is a blessing in progress.
Churches end in different ways. Some use Numbers. Some use Paul: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all."
Some add the sign of the cross.
And often, a few last words: go in peace.

how: Christian services often end with a benediction: the minister or priest raises a hand or both hands over the congregation and speaks a blessing, often Numbers 6:24–26 or 2 Corinthians 13:14, sometimes with the sign of the cross, followed by a dismissal such as "go in peace."

o: the last hymn the congregation sings together
a blessing spoken over people as a service ends
a prayer asking forgiveness before communion

p: the LORD bless thee, and keep thee
the first line of the blessing

s: the blessing in Numbers was first written for Christian churches
it was given to Aaron and his sons to bless Israel. Jews pray it still.
in Luke, Jesus is blessing the disciples as he's parted from them
"while he blessed them, he was parted from them."
in Numbers, the priest is the source of the blessing
the priests put God's name on the people, and God says, "I will bless them."

games.q: you're one of the disciples near Bethany, near the end of Luke's Gospel. Jesus is about to be parted from you. what is he doing?
o: lifting up his hands and blessing you.
giving instructions for building a church.
games.why: "he lifted up his hands, and blessed them." in Luke, the last thing the disciples see is a blessing still under way.

practice: Lift one hand a little, palm out, toward one person heading into a hard day: a friend before a test, a parent in a hospital.

If you pray, say the old words over them, one line per breath: the LORD bless thee, and keep thee; the LORD make his face shine upon thee; the LORD give thee peace. If you don't, wish them those three things your own way.

wordCard.voice: Benediction. A blessing spoken over people, often the words from Numbers, spoken as people leave.

orig.note: Hebrew: may he bless thee, the first word of the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24.

carryVoice: Your line: go in peace. The room empties into the week, blessed. See you tomorrow.
